This research focuses on creating resilient M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, with applications in both fault-tolerant and multi-qubit operations. By leveraging a variety of motionally coupled resonances, this system achieves balanced operation under fluctuating coefficients, ensuring that the gate remains stable even in response to significant changes. To optimize performance, coordinating the one-dimensional Doppler shifts associated with each ion is crucial; this is particularly important during delayed conditional phases, which can otherwise lead to unreliable results. To address this challenge, this study introduces a novel method using balanced contributions from multiple motionally coupled resonances, which rescues this failure and makes the gate stable once more. Furthermore, this finding also highlights the potential for phase modulation, both deep and shallow, as well as the secure execution of quantum swarm algorithms in environments prone to noise.

In perovskite materials, polarization origins are intricately intertwined, 
derived from two primary sources: symmetry lowering and lattice distortion. 
To dissect these effects, we developed the Conceptual Space Approach, 
combining extensive parameter spaces with critical evaluations to identify 
underlying causal relationships between properties and structures. Utilizing 
this method for paraelectric perovskites across 11 dimensions, we pinpoint 
the specific structural features responsible for dielectric breakdown and 
polarization, distinguishing between extrinsic (lattice distortion) and 
sufficient (tilting) contributions. Our analysis reveals distinct 
regional behaviors within the property spaces and uncovers the intricate 
relationships between structure, property, and performance, which can be 
influenced by subtle adjustments to chemical composition, lattice size, 
and atomic bond lengths.

In layered transition metal oxides, we have introduced a new class of materials, centered around Na$_3$V$_2$O$_2$ that exhibit strongly correlated physics within a Dirac cone. These materials have a unique three-dimensional structure, necessitating a comprehensive understanding derived from interlocking in-plane and out-of-plane bands. This knowledge allows us to predict that these materials will enter a quantum phase transition at sufficiently low temperatures, potentially giving rise to superconductivity, as predicted by a mean-field theory. This prediction is supported by early experimental findings. Building upon this foundation, we have identified Na$_3$V$_2$O$_2$ as a prime candidate for exploring the interplay between correlation-driven band reconstruction and superconductivity within the Dirac cone.

In our proposed framework, we address an unexplored area in bimodal analysis by developing a statistical method that utilizes bimodal data to estimate parameters in a proportion or rate. This framework builds on previous work using single-mode distributions and enables the incorporation of bimodal data into classic proportion estimation problems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through a simulation study and apply it to a real-world scenario, ultimately creating a comprehensive framework for bimodal rates and proportions.

Researchers explored the capabilities of the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance restrictions on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, specifically related to the interaction between a particular lepton and heavy neutral particles. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production searches lack in depth. Combining existing data with optimized detection tools or improved photon rejection techniques can significantly narrow this limit.

In a Sagnac interferometer, typically used for detecting gyrosopic effects, a phenomenon called spectral shift anomaly occurs when optical pulses within the interferometer move in opposite directions. This anomaly results in the inversion of spectral lines during operation, which poses a challenge in the development of Sagnac gyrosopes as it necessitates a sophisticated optical system to separate the interfering signals. Furthermore, this anomaly presents a quantum nonlocality manifestation, showcasing the entanglement between optical pulses moving in opposite directions and highlighting the inequivalence of the forward and backward spectral lines. Consequently, this anomaly arises due to the interaction of optical pulses with changing local frames of reference rather than gyrosopic effects.

In type $A$, the parabolic conjugacy class of a Borel subgroup contains other subgroups of the same type. This paper expresses the number of such conjugates using the Langlands parameter and Weil-Deligne scattering matrix. It also identifies specific conjugates, known as Weierstrass components, based on their relationship with the nilpotent subgroup of the Lie algebra. By analyzing this relationship, the paper determines the number of Weierstrass components for a given Langlands parameter. This number is shown to be at least the number of components in the nilpotent fibre, and in some cases, it is shown that this number is exactly the nilpotent fibre components, providing a solution to this problem for the first time. The proof involves a non-trivial use of the extended Cartan decomposition, as well as a detailed examination of the conjugacy class itself.

Neural language models have achieved significant success in text generation tasks.
However, in the Text Creation Task, our study reveals that the simple $n$-gram model
outperforms multiple neural models in a variety of settings.
To build upon this finding, we propose a residual learning model that combines
$n$-gram models with the benefits of neural language models.
The model integrates $n$-gram likelihood maximization to focus on rare words
and improves generalization by leveraging the extensive $n$-gram data.
In experiments, our results show that this approach not only surpasses
state-of-the-art neural models but also achieves superior performance in
downstream tasks and enhances the text quality in terms of diversity and
coherence. The model also facilitates few-shot learning by adapting to
new languages with zero-shot domain adaptation, achieving nearly identical
performance. The code for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramTCT.

We've developed new methods for analyzing $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties through the lens of mirror symmetry, specifically by extending Laurent inversion to a broader context. This enables us to explore non-toric $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties in dimension three, building on the work of Hacking, Katzarkov, Katzarkov, and Nemerov. Our approach also provides insights into varieties that are nearly $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano, offering potential solutions to computational problems in this area.

In recent years, 2D face alignment has achieved significant success due to the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), yet 3D face alignment and reconstruction remain a challenging task for everyday images despite the availability of abundant data, primarily because of the difficulty of obtaining precise correspondences for multiple facial points in the training set. This difficulty limits the construction of robust 3D face alignment and reconstruction models. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel method called SADRNet, which creates a bridge between 2D face alignment and 3D face reconstruction by utilizing a self-alignment mechanism in a dual face regression framework. This model allows 2D face alignment to be performed efficiently and effectively, while also enhancing the robustness of 3D face reconstruction. To train the model, we utilize a joint 2D-3D training strategy, which utilizes discriminative loss functions to focus on achieving precise correspondences for multiple facial points during training. The proposed method achieves superior performance to current state-of-the-art methods, according to evaluation results obtained using the widely used widely-used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets.

We demonstrate that translation symmetry breaking leads to an unusual aspect of field theory, known as a "fracton," where the speed at which some types of excitations are moved is significantly less than the speed of light. This particular phenomenon arises in a specific, widely applicable class of models that incorporate shifts in space or time. These models, which include cosmologically relevant theories that break spatial translations, can efficiently describe situations where one or more dimensions are significantly smaller than others. It has recently been proven that fractons inevitably result from models that spontaneously break translation symmetry in more than one dimension. In this study, we thoroughly examine the underlying mechanisms that give rise to these low-moving-dofermions in two-dimensional systems and explain how they cause an increased fine-tuning of the theory's parameters. We additionally present an example of a model that spontaneously breaks spatial translations in two dimensions, which can efficiently describe systems where one dimension is significantly smaller than another. It is shown that this model is equivalent to a system comprising low-moving-dofermions and massless particles, and it is proven that the speed of the low-moving-dofermions can be any fraction of the speed of light.

In an $\alpha$-attractor inflation model, we examine the behavior of perturbations during the early stages of inflation and beyond the transition from slow-roll to non-slow-roll dynamics. By directly solving the Klein-Gordon equation for the inflaton field and its perturbations, we gain a comprehensive understanding that extends past the slow-roll era. We then proceed to evaluate the likelihood of primordial black holes (PBHs) forming as a result of this process. In the non-slow-roll phase, where the potential becomes steeper, we observe that perturbations undergo amplification, increasing the risk of PBH formation. This enhancement becomes particularly pronounced in regions with more significant energy densities. Consequently, this results in a more significant fraction of the density fluctuation spectrum falling within the relevant amplification thresholds, increasing the predicted PBH abundance by several orders of magnitude in certain cases, where the density fluctuation sauce is quite sinusoidal.

In this study, we first establish the number of deepest vertices in a marked ordered tree of size n, denoted as a_n, for n greater than or equal to 2. Additionally, we derive the generating function G(x) for the sequence a_n as n varies from 0 to infinity.

This investigation seeks to examine the feasibility of using advanced optical character recognition (iOCR) techniques to accurately capture the contents of election ballot tallies displayed on various formats, such as paper-based systems, digital screens, or a combination of both. To achieve this, we propose an end-to-end iOCR system that combines sophisticated techniques to achieve high levels of reliability and efficiency. The proposed system differs from traditional OCR approaches, which typically require human input to correct predicted text, by utilizing a method that informs the model through contextual information derived from the input data. To evaluate the effectiveness of this system, we designed a context-informed training protocol that simulates the expected output by integrating the predicted text, thereby enabling the model to focus on making precise character predictions. Furthermore, we conducted a series of experiments to validate the performance of this system under various scenarios.

In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring multiple parameters. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in the context of low-data settings, with the goal of establishing whether such models can effectively utilize all available parameters. In this study, a linear regression model was utilized in a time series framework with an optimization procedure that utilizes stochastic gradient descent on a rolling window approach. The model was subsequently scaled up using synthetic data to examine its properties and behavior. The study discovered that models with excessive parameters have the ability to avoid significant overfitting by incorporating useful features, even in settings with limited data. The ability of these models to achieve this result is thought to be a consequence of incorporating inherent characteristics of time series data. The findings of this study may imply that models with excessive parameters can be preferable in settings with limited data, as they are capable of avoiding the detrimental effects of feature leakage while utilizing the implicit structure of time series data.

To improve deep learning-based single-channel speech enhancement, our proposed Attention Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Network (AB-RNN) model offers a novel complex architecture. By incorporating a bidirectional concept into a simple RNN structure, we increase the model's depth to better model the temporal coherence of audio signals. In addition, we introduce a groundbreaking all-encompassing attention mechanism to provide comprehensive focus across both past and future audio inputs. In our experiments, the AB-RNN model yielded notable improvements in the frequency domain short-time objective intelligibility measure (SIDRi) when compared to baseline models using the WSJ2SI mixture model and the Freebank dataset.

Bioscapers, members of a subculture that combines biology and hacking, have been actively promoting harm to society and themselves through dangerous science experiments, which are often accompanied by music videos showcasing these experiments. While initially viewed as absurd by law enforcement and medical professionals, these experiments have been successfully implemented by bioscapers, resulting in severe injuries and even deaths. Furthermore, the ease of accessing harmful information on the internet has enabled bioscapers to rapidly share their knowledge and coordinate their efforts. In this regard, the internet has transformed their dangerous activities from isolated incidents to global threats. In order to combat this emerging danger, it is essential for authorities to recognize the threat posed by bioscapers and the internet-facilitated spread of deadly ideas.

We're analyzing a multi-period market system with storage capabilities, featuring decentralized competition and bilateral contracts between firms. Our model incorporates risk-averse decision-making and utility maximization, and we demonstrate that there is an optimal self-allocation of storage within the market system. By leveraging the geometry of convex structures, we derive efficient computational methods for resolving equilibrium solutions. Additionally, our model can accommodate various types of risk aversion and valuation functions, and we provide specific examples of equilibrium solutions for both.

In quantum systems, superpositions of electronic states rapidly evolve, 
within the timeframe of few femtoseconds to attoseconds, leading to a charge 
density that varies over time. This work takes advantage of newly produced, 
ultrafast soft x-ray pulses generated by an x-ray free-electron laser to create 
an excitation of core electrons in nitric oxide molecules. Additionally, 
application of an infrared laser pulse in a circular polarization enables the 
creation of a reference point, thus enabling us to study the motion of electrons 
over time and, ultimately, modify this motion by adjusting the photon energy of 
the x-ray pulse. Systems in a state of core excitation provide a crucial framework 
for exploring the coherent electron evolution in matter with a high degree of 
excitation and strong interelectronic correlations.

A simplified computer model is used to study various atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating global wind patterns. The model, which focuses on high-speed wind patterns, is employed in three different geographical settings - a rotating sphere, a rotating sphere with obstacles, and an oblate rotating sphere. In the first scenario, the model produces a fast wind pattern seen in gas planets, while in the second, it exhibits multiple wind patterns similar to those observed in tropical regions of gas planets. The third scenario replicates atmospheric circulation patterns found on a methane-rich version of Mars with a thick atmosphere, displaying a transition from fast wind patterns to those similar to those on Mars as the atmospheric methane content is reduced.

Deep convolutional networks trained on large, labeled datasets like ImageNet deliver high performance and have become a benchmark for other training data. However, ImageNet's 1.3 million unlabeled test images haven't been utilized fully, representing valuable visual data that could further enhance training. We discovered several key challenges in using the test images for training, including poorly classified classes, inconsistent class labels, and narrow class distributions. To overcome these obstacles, we developed Dynamic Learning at the ImageNet Scale, a framework that allows for efficient, high-quality training on a reduced subset of labeled data. By incorporating a visual classification loss with a unique synthetic data augmentation technique, as well as a dynamic classifier that expands to match the scope of the training data, we achieved remarkable results. Our technique used just 125,000 labeled images and still matched the original ImageNet's 45% top-1 accuracy on the test set, a record at the time. Moreover, DLINS outperformed the original performance by 3% with only 125,000 labeled images, compared to using the entire ImageNet dataset.

In this work, we distill the underlying principles of the generalized algebraic multiplicity method proposed in [arXiv:2104.01333,  arXiv:2208.02922] for developing higher-order Lagrange-Hamilton operators. We demonstrate that this method simplifies the construction of Noether symmetries and conserved quantities for mechanical systems governed by higher-order Lagrange-Hamilton equations with involution. We illustrate the application of the generalized algebraic multiplicity in [arXiv:2208.02922] by deriving new, independent Noether symmetries and conserved quantities for the Einstein-Maxwell field equations. Furthermore, we advocate for the use of geometric structures as a unifying framework that facilitates the application of the generalized algebraic multiplicity.

We propose an method for creating bosonic pairs using large numbers of dipoles with interactions, which involve combining two sections of a fiber in a cavity. A specific optical field then causes these dipoles to react in a particular way, resulting in the entanglement of the pairs. We also explain how applying a classical field to the fiber can make the effect of these pairs more pronounced, which could be used for optical phase detection. Additionally, we show that this process shares some similarities with a squeezing operation, which is a fundamental step in certain quantum computing processes.

Researchers who utilize silicon-based quantum computing technologies have an important consideration: identifying and utilizing natural occurrences of two-valley entanglement in silicon, specifically within pairs of phosphorus atoms. These pairs can exhibit unique properties of quantum entanglement, as demonstrated through the exchange-coupling effect, which potentially uses the natural variation in energy levels for charge qubit operations. To effectively utilize this phenomenon, it is crucial to control the two-valley entanglement and related energy variations. To this end, a method of simulation has been developed, utilizing a comprehensive approach that takes into account the complex structure of silicon's energy variance. This method simulates the entire electronic configuration of pairs of phosphorus atoms, across various orientations, and across the natural variations in silicon, including the minima in energy levels. Through this method, it has been shown that the two-valley entanglement can be controlled through applied electric fields, potentially providing a means of managing this phenomenon.

Our investigation reveals that HgTe quantum wells, near the critical thickness where the gap between the conduction and valence bands closes, exhibit exceptionally high and stable conductivity when filled with electrons.  This conductivity maximization is achieved when the Fermi level is positioned at the bottom of the conduction band and we demonstrate that electron mobility within these samples can be very high, primarily due to reduced localization of electrons.  By filling the conduction band, we were able to enhance conductivity by comparing it to the same process with CuPhc nanoparticles where the conduction band is not fully occupied, resulting in lower conductivity as expected.  Furthermore, by studying the angle-dependent conductivity, we were able to gather further evidence that these samples behave like perfect conductors of electrons. Wireless communication systems can make significant contributions to preventing road accidents through alert message transmission, particularly in high-risk areas like road intersections. Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has shown promise for 5G systems, and our proposed adaptive cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol enhances VC's performance in this area. In a scenario where vehicles on intersecting roads generate interfering signals, we develop a mathematical model to evaluate the system's safety impact and provide analytical formulas for the reliability of alert messages at junctions. Through simulations, the ACN protocol's better performance is demonstrated, with improved message reliability at junctions, particularly in areas where vehicles are traveling at higher speeds.

In our research, we're addressing an adaptive challenge in 5G cell scheduling, as we've formulated a static solution method to consider non-cooperative game theory, yet this approach doesn't effectively capture the dynamics of 5G communication under stress. To overcome this limitation, we've developed an dynamic model for time division deceptively, mirroring the structure of its static counterpart, but with a response mechanism that adjusts to changing performance metrics and inter-cell interference levels. This new model allows us to leverage the knowledge of static solutions, exploiting their insights to devise efficient and robust scheduling policies, even in complex scenarios. Moreover, we've validated our method with numerical experiments, demonstrating a significant performance gain of up to 50% improvement in spectral efficiency over traditional static scheduling techniques.

In certain superconductors, the Hall anomaly is significantly affected by vacancies by destroying the long-range chiral order, which is in line with the vortex-lattice model. This study presents a quantitative analysis of the vortex matter in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{y}$ and Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{x}$ superconductors, based on measurements of the transverse magnetization at various temperatures and vortex densities. Our calculation shows that the vacancy-induced destruction of the long-range chiral order is more pronounced in Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{x}$ than in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{y}$. This difference in behavior is attributed to varying vortex pinning in the two materials. On the basis of magnetization measurements, it can be inferred that in both materials, the Hall anomaly is only negligible at very high temperatures. Additionally, the relationship between the chiral order and the density of vacancies was found to be directly proportional. In the context of the vortex-lattice model, the proportionality constant was found to be sensitive to temperature, potentially due to changes in the vortex radius or condensation energy.

Researchers propose using the moment approach to study critical phenomena, especially for experimental data that lacks high resolution near the critical point. Moments of a physical observable of a system are analyzed to identify the universality class by determining their behavior at the critical point. It has been observed in two-dimensional systems that the moments exhibit a fixed point at the critical point, exhibiting a minimum or a maximum according to even or odd order, respectively. In three-dimensional systems within the Ising universality class, including the case studied here which involves magnetic impurities on the surface of a three-dimensional Ising antiferromagnet, the moment approach was used for analysis. However, the behavior of the moments at the critical point was not as expected, with odd order moments not reaching a fixed point and being dominated by logarithmic divergences, and even order moments displaying a minimum but at a value greater than one. Therefore, alternative methods must be used in conjunction with theory for validation of the moment approach in experimental identification of critical exponents.

A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares that generate a type-II$_1$ subfactor of finite depth, specifically in relation to the index and depth, is achieved by establishing the equivalence of such squares to the standard one, $\boxtimes_0$, based on the property of generating a subfactor with central series. Additionally, this characterization is shown to apply more broadly to commuting squares of von Neumann algebras under certain conditions.

In this work, we employ Hamiltonian Neural Networks (hamNNs) to derive the differentiation of scalar functions w.r.t. a specific variable. We leverage the reverse mode of differentiation of the hamNN's training process, resulting in a computational graph where the derivatives of the output with respect to the input can be efficiently calculated. We demonstrate that this leads to a feasible computational problem by comparing it to the full training of the hamNN. Consequently, we can calculate the derivative of the predicted output with respect to the input for free. We utilize this property to enhance the training of hamNNs via the inclusion of the predicted derivatives of the loss function, leading to an increase in their performance. Additionally, hamNNs become capable of processing data with missing attributes by means of predicted derivatives. Our method achieves superior results to existing approaches in multiple benchmark experiments.

Simply updating machine learning models using existing data can sometimes backfire by reinforcing their flaws. To effectively utilize new data while preventing the model from devolving due to unexpected information, a collaborative approach is presented that combines the expertise of multiple agents. This method involves real-human input to regulate the model's performance by setting a threshold for reliability, creating a score that reflects how trustworthy the model is, and using new data to boost the score while preventing overfitting. The proposed system was tested on a scenario where it was trained to recognize images and control a robot, and the results showed that it was more efficient at raising the reliability score than a method that only updated the model directly.

In x-ray image analysis, particularly in detecting prohibited items, our proposed Lateral Inhibition Module aims to enhance performance by using lateral connections to focus attention on critical regions. Through experimentation on a newly established high-quality dataset called BPSD, our approach demonstrates superior detection capabilities compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. The BPSD dataset is a comprehensive benchmark consisting of 1500 images divided into three categories: airplane, gun, and bomb parts, collected from real-world airport x-ray exams. Our model achieves impressive results on this dataset, outperforming existing solutions with improved precision, recall, and AUC for each class. Through visualization, we show that our model effectively focuses on subtle details. The enhanced performance and the comprehensive nature of the BPSD dataset make it an reliable benchmark for evaluating and developing Prohibited Items Detection algorithms.

We introduce a novel, universally quantized invariant for links in a thickened torus. This invariant is constructed from a combination of the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus and a specific unitary operator from the Uq quantum torus. The invariance of this quantum invariant is confirmed, using the Volume Hypothesis, for a particular link that exhibits growth in both its real and imaginary spectrum. Moreover, we establish that this quantum invariant achieves its global minimum value among all links in the torus, thereby providing the first instance of a quantized, universally defined invariant that behaves in accordance with the Volume Hypothesis.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to incorporate contextual information for enhanced performance.  One effective method to add contextual information is through the use of graphs, which can provide a comprehensive understanding of words and their relationships.  However, building such graphs from scratch can be a challenging and time-consuming process.  To circumvent this issue, we propose creating contextual glosses, which are concise statements providing the meaning of a word's context.  We demonstrate that contextual glosses can enhance the performance of WSD tasks, with the added benefit of contributing valuable word sense information that can be reused for other NLP applications.

The converse of the digamma function, often denoted by $\Psi^{-1}(x)$, has multiple definitions, but a consensus on its behavior not bounded by $x$ has yet to be reached. In this study, we examine regularized integral expressions of the reciprocal gamma function from 1948, covering definitions proposed by Watson, Havil, and others, with a focus on their connections and distinguishing characteristics. We demonstrate that the standardization of these definitions is essential for a function to display the standard gamma function's properties. In the process, we present a definition that meets all conventional criteria and discuss various connections and inequalities derived from the studied definitions.

This letter reports on the search for top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions using 0.99 tev proton beams and various nuclear targets with a 13 tev center-of-mass energy. The data were collected with the LHC and analyzed using the ATLAS detector to search for the signature of top quark creation in the form of an electron or a muon, along with other particles, within specific energy ranges. Although the measured signal does not exceed the minimum required for the indicated process, it establishes limits on the cross-sectional area of the reaction, specifically for the production of a top quark and the subsequent decay into an electron and a jet, which is less than 11 fb^-1 with a 95% confidence level. Additionally, this study provides the first empirical value for the total cross-sectional area of proton-nucleus collisions, which is relevant to interpreting future discoveries in this area with larger data sets.

This study focuses on key elements in text-to-SQL tasks, specifically schema, table and value inference, and offers a novel framework to tackle these elements across different data sets. The proposed framework utilizes a single model to handle both in-domain and cross-domain tasks, leveraging an auxiliary task to enhance its ability to understand the semantic of text. In testing the framework on the SparkSQL dataset, it achieved superior performance when compared to baseline models for both in-domain and cross-domain text-to-SQL tasks.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the context of network data. It outlines the challenges posed by complex data structures and presents the various techniques developed to date, including private query execution, mutation-based approaches, and learning methods. Additionally, it highlights the limited body of research focused on network data and highlights key difficulties in this field, concluding that a framework combining graph algorithms and machine learning would address many of the existing challenges.

The vast image database and operating frequency of Euclid's near-infrared detectors make them ideal for conducting cultural heritage site detection and existing structure identification, particularly in previously unimaged areas. By examining pre-launched technical specifications and anticipated mission performance, we outline the capabilities and challenges of using Euclid for this purpose. Given its sensitivity, Euclid can detect and record even slight alterations, such as shifts in the spectral energy or movement, which could aid heritage site protection and management. To optimize results, we suggest that in-depth analytical techniques, such as model-based data processing, spectral matching, and change detection, be developed and implemented in the analysis of the data.

In this research, we propose an automatic method to create complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a method to generate high-quality paths, we can prevent issues with unnatural turns and intersections, ensuring a more realistic and challenging testing environment. To further increase the difficulty, we incorporate random obstacles into the network, allowing us to evaluate the system's performance in various challenging scenarios. This approach enables us to generate road networks in a short amount of time, allowing for rapid iteration and system refinement. We validate our method by testing an implemented search algorithm on the generated networks.

To facilitate user discovery in music recommendation, visual representations like album art are commonly employed; however, these fall short in effectively conveying the content of a music playlist. To address this limitation, we introduce music captioning, a novel application that leverages text to describe music playlists. In this initial study, we assemble a large-scale dataset, develop a pioneering captioning framework, and conduct experiments to demonstrate its feasibility. The obtained results not only outperform a straightforward comparative approach but also showcase a genuine improvement in performance. To facilitate further exploration in this new area, we release both the dataset and code in conjunction with this presentation.

Researchers have long used hydrodynamic theories to describe complex fluids in high-temperature environments, and in quantum systems, a similar approach shows promise, especially with recent experiments involving ultracold atom clouds. These experiments involve highly interacting Bose gases at temperatures low enough to exhibit quantum properties. Due to the low density of these systems, standard hydrodynamic theories based on continuous phase-space fields are not applicable as they typically require a high density of particles to ignore empty phase-space. Instead, a new quantum hydrodynamic theory has been developed that takes into account the random fluctuations of phase-space fields and accurately captures the unique characteristics of low-density, interacting Bose gases. Notably, this new theory predicts that certain non-hydrodynamic correlations will decay much more slowly as time passes, providing a key signature that can be experimentally verified.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for temporal action detection, which simultaneously tackles proposal coherence and semantic distinctness. DCAN aggregates context from two sources: local context (LC) and group context (GC). LC is used to refine proposals through backpropagation during boundary matching, while GC is employed to generate initial proposals by aggregating context from multiple groups. To prevent proposal overlap, a matching metric is applied during both boundary matching and proposal grouping. Experiments show that our method achieves superior performance on the ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14 datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods by a significant 3.2% and 12.5% in average recall at 0.5, 5, 10, and 50 frames per second (FPS) on ActivityNet v1.3 and 1.1% and 5.6% mean average precision at different FPS on THUMOS-14.

The theory of palm tree structures in plasma remains unsolved, and a commonly accepted explanation in the edge plasma community posits that these unique patterns are linked to a particular EAC mode. In our study, we contradict this widely accepted theory by presenting evidence that palm tree modes are actually instances of island structures, resulting from the interaction of two nearby and nearly congruent magnetic surfaces in the diverted region of the JET tokamak. This interpretation is based on the observation that the location of palm tree patterns shifts in response to changes in the lower side of the rice-shaped area, and is not affected by upper boundary, as would be expected if they were related to a specific EAC mode. In addition, our study includes an advanced numerical model that accurately identifies the island structure of a palm tree pattern observed during a plasma discharge on JET, where the distance between the two interacting surfaces is extremely close, making it imperceptible on typical magnetic spectrum diagrams.

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for independent mobile robots moving dynamically in a shared environment. To achieve this, a novel approach is introduced using dynamic vortex potential fields that work in harmony with each other. This method ensures that the movement of one robot does not cause the other to move into a dangerous situation, making it an effective solution for collision avoidance. This approach is also adaptable to a variety of situations, including paths that loop back on themselves, and has been successfully tested on robots that move dynamically in a simulated environment and on actual robots with wheels.

Consider a long sequence of letters generated from a source text, where the letter combinations are drawn at random according to a pre-specified probability distribution. If the source text is rich and diverse, establishing a central limit theorem for the average of local statistics within the sequences becomes increasingly challenging due to their potentially low degree of independence. Similarly, obtaining a large deviation principle for the averaged statistics faces a similar obstacle. In this study, we develop a new method for obtaining a large deviation principle for a class of averaged statistics that can handle a limited degree of correlation between the letter combinations. This achievement is then applied to derive a central limit theorem for a specific type of averaged statistic. The large deviation principle can also be applied to a scenario where the source text itself is drawn at random from a given distribution, enabling us to obtain a large deviation principle for the average of statistics drawn from a random text. This research was motivated by problems in language modeling, specifically word ordering, where establishing a large deviation principle was a key goal.

The incorporation of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) into radar systems has tremendous potential to increase target parameter estimation accuracy. By actively adjusting their reflections, IRS can reformulate the radar signal scattering problem, potentially resolving target identification issues due to polarization and shape ambiguities. This paper investigates the integration of IRS with MIMO radars, presenting a mathematical model that accounts for complex signal processing and surface behavior. MUltiplexed Optimal-Weighted Coherently Integrated (MOWC) is an innovative method for combining radar signals and IRS weights, capable of optimizing target parameter estimation. The problem of finding optimal MOWC weights is reformulated as a constrained convex problem, solvable through efficient optimization techniques. Furthermore, the paper examines the advantages of the IRS-supported radar, demonstrating a significant improvement in target parameter estimation and robustness to polarization and shape ambiguities.

Fuzzers are commonly used testing tools for software, designed to identify and exploit flaws to ensure the security and stability of the program. Although widely applied, the underlying principles of fuzzing remain poorly understood, hindering its effective use and limiting the development of higher-level testing techniques. This study provides a theoretical foundation for the underlying concepts of fuzzing, consisting of generating diverse input data to test the robustness of software for specific purposes. Based on this foundation, the authors develop novel techniques for comparing fuzzers that quantify the diversity of generated input, along with strategies for selecting and evaluating diverse inputs to guide the testing process. These advancements lead to the development of advanced techniques for selecting the most effective fuzzer, based on its ability to discover flaws, its efficiency, and its ability to produce diverse inputs, even in the presence of significant performance bottlenecks.

Pretrained models have been highly effective in adapting to new tasks in few-shot learning settings, and their integration with continuation learning methods has yielded promising results. Notably, a study found that using a combination of both approaches - continuation learning methods with pretrained models - consistently outperformed other configurations. However, it has also been observed that in some cases, simply re Freezing the pretrained model's weights from previous tasks can be beneficial, which may indicate that continuation learning methods are unnecessary in certain situations. This phenomenon prompted us to conduct a more in-depth examination, and interestingly, we found that in many scenarios, reheating the weights alone performs at least as well as, and sometimes even better than, combining continuation learning methods with pretrained models. This counterintuitive finding challenges the need to continue learning new methods in sequential tasks and suggests that weighted aggregation might be an effective continuation learning strategy. To further explore this concept, we introduced a simple baseline that involves calculating the average of the logits from previous tasks, which can be adapted to accommodate an arbitrary number of previous tasks. This baseline outperformed the state-of-the-art continuation learning methods with pretrained models in our experiments, and it particularly showed significant improvement in datasets with diverse classes.

In this research, we establish a homotopy theorem for surfaces minimizing area in a given metric space, within a specified homotopy class. Our proof does not rely on subdifferential properties but rather on a localized version of the Ekeland variational principle. Consequently, this homotopy theorem holds applicable to any complete metric space.

This final installment concludes our comprehensive study of the solutions $u$ to the given semilinear parabolic equation on the real line. These bounded solutions $u$ of the equation $u_t = u_{xx} + f(u)$, where the initial data are convergent to distinct limits, exhibit oscillatory behavior near infinity as time progresses. If $x$ and time are scaled appropriately, the solution can be redefined to approach a non-constant periodic equilibrium directly, as demonstrated in an earlier companion study. However, if $x$ and time are scaled in a different way, the solution can be redefined to approach a non-constant periodic equilibrium after a significant delay, as shown in another companion study. However, if the scaling factors are set to $\epsilon$ and $1/\epsilon$ respectively, the solution can be redefined to approach a non-branching equilibrium at the origin, while approaching a non-branching periodic equilibrium at a divergent limit.

Recent studies on 64Ni, performed using combinations of electrons, protons, and gamma rays, have revealed coexisting shapes in this nucleus for the first time since 66Zn was explored.  By examining energy patterns and comparing them to theoretical predictions, researchers found that 64Ni exhibits both spherical and prolate shapes, with the latter being particularly prominent in rotations around the short axis.  This finding challenges previous theories that 64Ni's ground state is an excited prolate rotation, and sheds new light on the complex interplay of forces that shape this nucleus.  A strong monopole force is responsible for driving the competition between these shapes, with implications for understanding similar phenomena in other nuclei.

Approximately nine years ago, a significant breakthrough occurred, establishing the existence of nearly optimal pure mixed strategies in games with continuous actions and payoffs that exhibit limited variability. This landmark result, based on the concept of a Lipschitz game, was a significant achievement, yet the current inquiry aims to accelerate progress in this field by which specific payoffs can be efficiently identified, allowing for the efficient finding of equilibrium payoffs, even if only approximately. This study leverages a recently developed metric, the Lipschitz dimension of a payoff, to achieve this goal, providing an alternative approach that is both more flexible and more complicated to evaluate. Moreover, the current research introduces new lower bounds for the complexity of finding equilibrium payoffs, which are based on both the Lipschitz dimension and the complexity of the game's action space, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the query complexity of finding equilibrium payoffs. It is also demonstrated that in certain scenarios, such as zero-sum games and games with variable complexity, the current limits can be exceeded, while in other scenarios, such as the finding of correlated equilibria, the established lower bounds can be achieved with a specific approach, resulting in a more detailed analysis of the complexity of finding equilibrium payoffs.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are often insensitive to the method used, with their selection being heavily influenced by the inherent characteristics of the evaluation metric and the data set at hand. Consequently, we advocate for the use of J-k fold CV, a method that accounts for the inherent data structure and reduces the degree of freedom involved in model assessment. In the context of NLP, we observed that adopting a method that considers the inherent data structure results in significantly more stable performance estimates than traditional CV. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of selecting an appropriate evaluation metric, with some metrics being more robust than others in relation to the choice of parameters.

In recent years, teacher-student architectures have become the primary method for training neural networks using limited labeled data, due to their effectiveness in combining both efficient inference and robust training. This trend is particularly evident in data-efficient training for machine learning, where the need to convey rich semantic information from a trained model to a trainable network has created research opportunities in both machine learning and computer vision. To explore these opportunities, our survey delves into teacher-student architectures from a knowledge learning perspective, covering key concepts, techniques, applications, and future challenges in this knowledge transmission paradigm.

We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which significantly speeds up finding the maximum probability expectation (MPE) solution by limiting the expected value to a certain range. Our method quickly finds exact MPE solutions even in large datasets, reducing the computational time by several orders of magnitude. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to image segmentation, a complex problem often solved using graphical models, and the MPE objective. Our technique achieves this efficiency gain without the need for approximate algorithms or expensive message passing calculations.

The interaction between an intense laser beam and a cold gas of atoms offers a setting to examine the photon recoil effect in detail. We employed single-beam absorption spectroscopy, monitored by detection of absorption imbalances, to investigate the influence of photon recoil on absorption patterns. Our study specifically utilized an ultracold strontium gas and showed that certain conditions can make the recoil effect as significant as other absorption-related phenomena. We derived a precise method to extract the photon recoil parameter $\kappa$ by analyzing the distribution of absorption imbalances. Our measurement yields a value of $2.10 \times 10^{-5}$, and we found that it adheres to the prediction of quantum mechanics in scenarios where the photon momentum is minimal.

When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of liquid materials undergo a sudden and dramatic transition from low viscosity to high viscosity behavior, characterized by the development of solid-like properties. This phenomenon, which the researchers call "shear thickening," is uniquely evident in cornstarch when high speeds are applied. Unlike other fluids with shear thickening behavior that have been studied extensively, cornstarch exhibits noticeable changes in its physical appearance during the transition from low to high viscosity states. Utilizing high-speed cameras to observe rice flour suspensions similar to cornstarch, and combining the findings with existing data on cornstarch, the study measures the scaling of the shear thickening transition in terms of stress, distance traveled by neighboring particles, and how it relates to the size of the particles. Based on their data, the researchers propose that the transition occurs when the stress is high enough to cause particles to collide repeatedly, resulting in an unpredictable movement that ultimately leads to the clustering of particles during the transition. Moreover, the findings suggest that the transition becomes more distinct as the size of the particles decreases, to the point where the distinction disappears at some critical point, potentially linked to the failure of fluid fluids to hold their shape.

We introduce the Racah algebra, an extension of the Askey-Wilson algebra, which has previously been referred to as the largest algebra in the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ family containing the Askey-Wilson algebra. We then establish that the centralizer of the group $U_n$ within the universal enveloping algebra of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of the Racah algebra for all $n \geq 2$. Furthermore, we identify this centralizer as the Racah algebra itself for $n = 2, 3$, while for $n \geq 4$, it is an extension of the Racah algebra, which we refer to as the extended Racah algebra. We also provide the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ for all $n \geq 2$.

Our study shows that in magnets with a bilayer hexagonal structure, which allows for the exchange of quantum properties between two layers, there is a unique opportunity for quantum mechanical, permanent triplon excitation that can provide a cold storage for revealing hidden features of this material. Notably, this excitation can transition into a liquid-like state that is twisted, as well as a perfectly ordered state that is supersolid, due to the interaction between the layers. The existence of these phenomena, which include a twisted superfluid and supersolid phase, can be detected by examining the patterns of isotope distribution, and they rely on the balance between two types of layer interactions: quantum correspondence and nearest neighbor interaction. Characteristically, the twisted superfluid phase exhibits random, harmonic vibrations between different order states, while the supersolid phase remains static in these states. Moreover, by adjusting the balance of these interactions, it is possible to switch between these phases that have distinct, quantum mechanical properties, potentially enabling the use of these materials for storing and revealing the unique features of these materials.

This study continues from a previous research on WIMP-nucleus interaction velocities by expanding the analysis to a 3-dimensional scenario. Initially, the velocity-recoil angle distribution of WIMP-nucleus interactions is further developed, revealing how the angle of recoil is influenced by the incident velocity, consistent with the findings of a preceding 1-dimensional study. Subsequently, the velocity-recoil angle distribution is analyzed from different perspectives, including the 90-degree angle, which indicates a direct velocity-EVRD relationship. A formula for the 90-degree EVRD is derived, showing how the recoil angle affects the energy spectrum of WIMP-nucleus interactions.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work is evident is in professional search for information. This study's desktop search environment's findings may not be fully transferable, as they reveal a significant Web search personalisation impact on finding relevant information. This study's results show that work-related information can be missed due to tailored search results, with as much as 42% of relevant information beyond the first page of search engine results not being viewed. This stress on Google to expand the visible search results or offer a work-related search section is backed up by this study's findings.

We are presenting a conceptual design for a cutting-edge muon collider with multiple capabilities, tailored to achieve groundbreaking discoveries in high-energy physics beyond the current TeV range. Considering potential challenges with conventional colliders, such as ground access limitations for extremely long detectors, we propose an innovative design that integrates the collider with sophisticated detectors in a teardrop-shaped lattice, allowing for more versatile experiments and better tolerance of muon decay modes. Additionally, we can utilize a small percentage of the available lattice and take advantage of naturally occurring muon transverse polarization to enhance sensitivity in specific processes. Furthermore, we can leverage a teardrop design with extremely long "tails" to facilitate unprecedented insights into rare processes involving muons and other particles at very low energies, a range that conventional detectors often struggle to access. We also outline two potential implementation phases, with initial prototype development focusing on TeV-scale energies and potential for direct physics, as well as subsequent construction of a fully capable collider with multiple purposes.

A new technique for capturing and analyzing respiratory motion in MRI has been developed, offering an improved alternative to previous methods. By maintaining constant flow regulation and image acquisition time, the new technique effectively eliminates variations in data collection, even in the presence of changing breath hold periods. As a result, data processing techniques such as image reconstruction and tumor tracking can rely on consistent parameters, leading to more accurate results. Furthermore, the technique enables the creation of high-quality, respiratory-phase-specific images for tumor assessment and other applications, potentially reducing the need for contrast agents and guiding procedures like radiotherapy and ablation, among other uses.

The concept of control barrier functions has been recently introduced to create controlled exit boundaries in forward thinking control for systems with state constraints. This research expands upon that concept by introducing the idea of control barrier functions with input constraints, capable of defining controlled boundaries in complex systems subject to input limitations, as seen in motors and other underactuated systems. The research demonstrates that by incorporating reference trajectories, such boundaries can be achieved through the application of control barrier functions with input constraints, as well as other feasible controls. Additionally, it demonstrates that by defining upper and lower boundaries, the system can be controlled to stay within those boundaries. The research also introduces the term "control boundary function" to simplify the notation, as well as the concept of discrete control barrier functions for their potential application in distributed control systems.

In the field of computer science, region-based representation has proven to be a versatile approach, applicable to various problems in image processing, geometry, and computer vision. This approach, however, poses a significant representation challenge, particularly in cases where regions do not conform to simple predicates. To address this challenge, we draw from the concept of continuous function approximations and introduce the idea of CF-spaces, which enables the representation of any function as a unique combination of elements from a set of continuous functions. Building on this foundation, we develop the CF-approximation model, which allows for the precise representation of mathematical regions through the use of algorithms based on $\epsilon$-approximations and $\delta$-approximations. This framework facilitates not only the expression of discrete regions in terms of continuous functions but also the reversal of this process, thereby demonstrating its generality and versatility. Through the use of CF-approximation, we can seamlessly integrate region-based reasoning with more traditional approaches to reasoning, such as the description-logics-based reasoning, thus making our approach not only theoretically sound but also practically viable.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, the paired-permutation test has consistently yielded unsatisfactory performance in previous studies. To address this issue, we first identify the underlying source of this problem as the inadequate handling of overlapping samples. We then propose a new, precise paired-permutation testing method that accounts for this issue. In experiments comparing NLP systems, our new testing method delivers significantly better performance than the existing alternative.

A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the six primary shipping routes. This dataset addresses the difficulty of procuring a full set of unified data for the shipping industry, enabling researchers to explore various phenomena and patterns observed in the industry. Several features make the dataset particularly useful: the coexistence of both competitive and monopolistic elements in the shipping market; the presence of significant fixed costs and variable costs that can be manipulated; the fact that shipping quantity is bounded by the available number of ships; and the unique price mechanisms specific to the shipping industry. Furthermore, the dataset has been tested for various empirical biases, and a series of simple models has been implemented to provide insight into the underlying behaviors that the data reflect. Specifically, the analysis reveals that the shipping industry exhibits characteristics of monopoly power during certain price fluctuations, and that the industry's response to changes in shipping quantity and freight rates follows a bounded pattern. Additionally, the data indicate that the construction of new ships is often driven by the promise of high profits, while the sale of used ships is often motivated by the need to reduce costs and minimize tax liabilities.

We define loom areas as a broader class of structures that incorporate veering triangulations, before establishing a biunivalent correlation between veering triangulations and loom areas on 3-dimensional closed oriented manifold triangulations. This connection is also shown to extend to non-orientable manifolds. Additionally, a method for automatically generating a loom area from a given surgery configuration is demonstrated, along with a reverse process using a loom area to derive that configuration. Furthermore, the relationship between loom areas and veering triangulations is shown to encompass isomorphisms, homeomorphisms, and more.

Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called learned sparsification for GNNs, which involves representing model connections as a minimal subset of key edges. These critical edges are selected based on optimized scores that reflect the importance of each edge in relation to the graph classification. We utilize this approach in a selected-edge graph sparsification framework, which involves repeatedly refining the selected edges and updating the node features. Our framework encompasses multiple scoring methods, including a score-based approach that utilizes the graph attention network, and our evaluations on diverse datasets highlight the effectiveness of our approach in achieving both high classification accuracy and interpretability of the models.

The CountSketch algorithm by Charikar for estimating the top k elements of a stream with the highest count is highly efficient, with a small memory footprint, but its effectiveness declines in response to adaptive operations performed on the stream, particularly when these operations are based on knowledge of CountSketch itself. Our research presents an extended version of CountSketch, called DynamicCountSketch, capable of handling not only independent arrivals but also adaptive operations, thereby retaining its efficiency. DynamicCountSketch achieves this by employing multiple instances of CountSketch with distinct parameters and using a limited amount of additional memory to prioritize the most frequent elements. Consequently, its space complexity is comprised of $\Omega(k/\Delta^2)$ entries, where $\Delta$ represents the greatest gap between the counts of any two elements, and its estimation time is $\mathcal{O}(k/\Delta^2)$, where $\Delta$ is the largest fraction of the total count held by any single element. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DynamicCountSketch maintains the same steady-state distribution as CountSketch and adapts seamlessly to any changes in the stream. Our innovative approach to DynamicCountSketch has far-reaching implications, as it offers an optimized solution for handling a wide range of streaming applications, including various variants of dynamic CountSketch, such as DynamicCountSketch with multi-counting, where each input corresponds to an individual count, as well as DynamicCountSketch for finding the minimum degree of a distribution.

Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature can be conformally deformed to reveal related minimal geometries sharing key characteristics. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets present in these geometries.

The Nernst effect is examined in a vortex liquid state of a type-II superconductor, with particular focus on its connection to viscosity and mobile entropy. It is found that in the vortex liquid state, the anomalous Nernst effect is dominated by a thermal gradient-induced magnetic field, which results in an unusual entropy distribution. This distribution differs from that in the normal state, the underlying cause of which is the interaction between a heat pulse and Abelian vortices. It is also found that in the vortex liquid state, the Hall conductivity is independent of temperature, whereas in the normal state, it is proportional to temperature. This distinction arises due to the varying spatial arrangements of vortices in different states. Additionally, it is observed that in the vortex liquid state, the normal and anomalous Nernst coefficients become equal, with the same value determined by the vortex density and the normal state conductivity. This equality of coefficients is a unique feature of the vortex liquid state, resulting from the close relationship between normal and anomalous transport processes in this state. It is suggested that in narrow channels or in thin films of type-II superconductors, the vortex liquid state may exhibit anisotropic viscosity, with the component along the superconducting channel or film resisting flow more than the transverse component. This anisotropic viscosity may lead to the entropic resistance experienced by moving charges in these systems.

Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to this challenge, in which real-time coordination is achieved through the exchange of sparse flexibility messages. We develop a state feedback controller that combines offline computation with online optimization, leveraging machine learning to reduce costly calculations, thereby minimizing communication between systems. Key benefits of this approach include decreased communication needs, improved efficiency of flexible resources, and better utilization of those resources. We demonstrate the performance of this scheme in a simulated study of home energy management.

The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning's ability to accurately predict time series data has been consistently demonstrated. In the realm of technical analysis, using indicators is the most widely adopted approach among traders and investors. Another essential aspect is sentiment analysis, reflecting the emotional state of investors' willingness to invest, where various techniques such as Machine Learning and Neural Networks have been employed. From simple linear regression to advanced neural networks, researchers and investors have experimented with multiple methods to forecast the stock market. It is evident from recent market fluctuations how news headlines and cryptocurrency prices are affected. This research paper presents an ensemble of state-of-the-art techniques to forecast stock values. It starts with applying a BERT-based sentiment analysis model to analyze the emotional state of Apple Inc investors listed on NASDAQ. A subsequent GAN-based model predicts the company's stock value based on technical indicators, global sentiment, and historical data. This approach results in a notable 20% increase in accuracy when compared to traditional methods.

We have developed a novel new method for creating envelope structures in numerical modeling, which can be applied across a broad spectrum of uses such as computational astrophysics, multi-material physics, and phase-field materials science. This new approach transforms the complexity of handling sharp interfaces and metamorphosing structures, making it possible for multiple substances to mix and vary in an envelope shape. By redefining how we handle diffusion and interface forces, this new formalism leverages the benefits of high-resolution methods near interfaces and provides a highly efficient way to model transitioning structures through a match kernel. In our implementation of this new framework in the high-resolution finite volume method, we've successfully modeled various patterns, such as the interaction of two colliding materials, a breaking wave, and a stable stellar envelope over a rotating star.

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs interactions. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the Higgs coupling modification, specifically the influence of new physics on the diphoton decay of the 125 GeV Higgs boson and the associated double Higgs production. We leverage the example of a TeV-scale leptoquark, which could plausibly lead to such signatures. To evaluate the sensitivity of the processes, we calculate the cross-sections for $pp$ and $e^+e^-$ collisions at TeV-scale energies as well as the relevant signatures at TeV-scale $e^+e^-$ colliders CLIC and ILC. Our research reveals that the planned CLIC and ILC data, which correspond to an integrated luminosity of 1 $ab^{-1}$, are sufficient to accurately determine the BSM contribution to the HEFT cross-section for the process $e^+e^-\to \gamma\gamma b\bar b$ at the 95% confidence level (C.L.) for energies above 230 GeV and 195 GeV, respectively.
