A comparison of observed core gas densities with predictions of the POPS model shows that there is a notable discrepancy, with the model indicating a more dense environment than actually exists, which could be related to how density is affected during the transition from direct formation to mergers. A further examination of this transition holds the key to understanding how massive stars are formed.

Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding mass-scale formation in quantum field theory. This paper explores the extension of this approach to wedge-local nets of observables in two-dimensional scattering theories. It demonstrates that any net of local observables in one-dimensional spectrum can be transformed into a wedge-local net through application of a natural endomorphism, as first proposed by Buchholz and Halbleib. This transformation preserves the property of local consistency. Additionally, in scattering theories defined by the Reeh-Schlieder property, any wedge-local net can be obtained from local nets via extension of natural endomorphisms, including those associated with wedge-local nets in one-dimensional spectra. This leads to the conclusion that in such cases, one-dimensional spectra are fundamental and cannot be derived from wedge-local nets in one-dimensional spectra.

Concerno, a Spanish non-profit organization, has collected and analyzed 5G emission data from base stations across Spain. These emissions, also known as radiofrequency fields, have been measured at various locations, including children's and teenagers' homes, schools, and hospitals. Concerno's findings show that the measured emission levels are often significantly higher than recommended limits set by the World Health Organization (WHO). For instance, measurements taken at 10 different schools ranged from 1.7 to 46.2 nanoseconds per meter (ns/m), with 5 out of 10 exceeding the 25 ns/m threshold. Similarly, measurements at 10 hospitals ranged from 0.5 to 50.1 ns/m, with 4 out of 10 exceeding the 25 ns/m threshold. Notably, measurements at children's and teenagers' homes varied greatly, spanning from 0.5 to 49.3 ns/m. It is essential to note that these measurements are site-specific and may differ from those in other countries with 5G networks. Furthermore, the organization suggests that open access to such data and the development of citizen science projects could facilitate more comprehensive monitoring and assessment of 5G emission levels.

This research develops a new Hamiltonian model, the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation, to predict and manage high-amplitude, irregular waves in an one-dimensional ocean channel with circulating water, a phenomenon commonly observed on coastlines. By assuming a linear water depth, H. Dysthe's method is used to derive an efficient, nonlinear model that takes into account the effects of water circulation. Unlike other methods, this new model maintains a Hamiltonian structure, which is beneficial as it ensures the model's predictions remain accurate even at very large amplitudes. By further analyzing the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation, we determine that it is a quasi-linear Hamiltonian PDE and therefore possesses stable solutions. To verify the model's effectiveness, we compare its predictions to actual wave measurements during heavy seas.

In this paper, we expand the concept of differential shapes on convex spaces to include those that are not necessarily convex. This expansion enables us to derive a modified version of the Stokes formula for differential forms within a specific type of space. Specifically, we define differential shapes on locally convex spaces and establish their connection to the Stokes formula in a very general setting. This achievement represents a significant expansion of the theory developed by J.H. Michael in his work on minimal surfaces within Euclidean spaces.

The development of sonar sensors for mobile robots has accelerated, leading to lower prices and more advanced technology. While the hardware advancements are noticeable, the development of processing software and signal interpretation still presents a challenge. This processing capability is essential for real-time navigation control using sonar sensors. To address this, a simple and effective method for integrating sonar sensors with navigation layers was developed, with the goal of providing mobile robots with better collision avoidance capabilities in dynamic environments. This approach was successfully demonstrated using a navigation system with infrared sensors and a mobile robot equipped with a 5MHz sonar sensor. The results showed a significant improvement in safety when navigating through a dynamic environment filled with moving obstacles.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages automated text summarization to detect false news. Our approach involves a summarization process to condense lengthy articles into concise summaries, which serve as indicative features of the content's credibility. By training a classification model on these summaries, we can effectively determine the content's validity. Our experiments demonstrate that this method is an efficient and reliable way to detect false news, outperforming traditional approaches.

We analyze the impact of bending on functional central limit theorems for stationary Gaussian processes and random fields. Depending on the type of embedding, different parameters such as the norm of the integral of the process, its supremum, or its tail behavior can be relevant. Our results apply to isotropic Gaussian fields in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and demonstrate that under certain conditions, for $d>2$, the standard functional central limit theorem can be obtained with fewer moment assumptions.

This research targets addressing the security concerns of non-contiguous multiple access techniques, particularly power-domain NOMA, which divides users into higher and lower power groups to facilitate decoding. Unprotected power-domain signals make it simple for eavesdroppers to obtain transmitting power information, which is then used to intercept messages. To overcome this challenge, this study proposes an encoding method, known as "decoded message indication," which informs intended recipients of successfully decoded information without revealing power levels or other sensitive information. Consequently, unwanted users will struggle to interpret the messages due to inadequate transmitting power, thus preventing unauthorized access. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method is an efficient solution for securing NOMA systems, outperforming conventional encoding methods by approximately 50% in terms of decoding failure rate and exceeding 90% successful decoding cases when the signal-to-noise ratio is 20dB.

We have developed an algorithm to identify the number of components in a data set's lowest dimensional rotationally invariant subspace, specifically when that subspace is defined by minimizing the $\ell_1$-norm of the coefficients. This algorithm achieves linear convergence when the data meets certain conditions and fails to converge otherwise. To optimize the algorithm, we employ a smoothing technique and a gradient-based method that converges within a certain distance when the data does not meet the required conditions. The algorithm can be applied to any rotationally invariant method, including PCA.

The significant success of BERT in various tasks has prompted numerous studies on its potential in tasks like text classification, sentence annotation, and question answering. As a result, BERT has been explored in various applications, including natural language processing tasks like sentiment analysis and text classification. In the field of special education, BERT-based models have improved sentiment awareness, but there is a lack of established standard protocol for evaluating models in this domain. The recent BERT-based studies in special education have primarily focused on developing models that can classify emotions and improve text comprehension. In contrast, the emphasis has shifted from text classification to semantic annotation in recent years. Semantic annotation involves labeling specific parts of the sentence with emotional connotations, making it a more intricate process than classification. Therefore, semantic annotation requires more precise guidance than classification. The recent studies on BERT and neural kraken have demonstrated potential improvements in annotation quality. However, there is a lack of studies on combining BERT and neural kraken to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of annotating emotion-related questions. In response to this gap, we developed a BERT-supported annotation guide, which incorporates neural kraken's capabilities to increase efficiency and effectiveness. The guide enables the rapid production of high-quality annotations even from untrained annotators. The results from the experiments showed significant improvements in annotation quality when compared to the traditional method. The findings from this study have the potential to accelerate the development of large-scale datasets for evaluating emotion-related question answering models. Additionally, the BERT

We create an original energy model that utilizes a powerful, ordered group to ensure competitive strategies lead to energy minimization, and we prove this approach achieves the optimal outcome. Additionally, we demonstrate this framework's versatility by applying it to both finite and infinite scenarios, as well as showing its relevance to familiar settings like $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and the real numbers.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence.

This study compares two approaches to integrating the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with a monolithic and a segmented solution strategy for solving Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) problems. Monolithic solving involves treating the fluid and solid components simultaneously, whereas segmented solving breaks down the process into sequential steps for the two components. High-dimensional RBM is used to efficiently handle multiple input parameters in both approaches. However, because the methods for deriving the reduced order models for the fluid and solid components differ, due to the respective uses of weak and strong approximations, considerable attention is devoted to their impact on overall performance. Specifically, we examine how the choice of approximation, solution strategy, and RBM approach, either monolithic or segmented, affects computational efficiency in terms of solution time, data storage, and overall feasibility. To this end, we employ a simplified model to derive the reduced order model, which facilitates more meaningful comparisons of the approaches under study.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having a reliable local navigation system is crucial. Currently available methods primarily focus on grid-based representations, which can, however, pose difficulties when attempting to translate them into a suitable format for path planning. In contrast, hierarchical representations show promise in capturing the topological properties essential for navigation. Unfortunately, existing approaches of this type, while effective, lack representation flexibility and are often limited to having a fixed number of levels. To address this shortfall, we present HiTMap, a novel representation that uses interconnected nodes with distinct radii to represent different environmental areas, making it an ideal system for incorporating sensory data from various sources. Furthermore, HiTMap features a dynamic structure, allowing it to adapt to changing conditions and incorporate new information. Through successful implementation on a simulation platform and real-world tests, we demonstrate HiTMap's capability to navigate through unfamiliar environments while maintaining a dynamic structure.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval Aggressive Detection Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect aggressive tweets by combining BERT and SVM models. BERT was utilized as a feature extractor for the dataset's initial analysis, and subsequently, an SVM classifier was trained and tuned to determine the most effective features leading to aggressive language. BERT's extracted features were then fed into an SVM classifier to achieve the best results, ultimately yielding a high macro F1 score of 42. Given the challenges of aggressive language, our simple approach yielded satisfactory results, and our code is publicly available for replication and further development.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A method for enhancing atomic interferometry's sensitivity to these fields is proposed, potentially enabling the realization of ultra-precise measurements. Basic superconducting loops' characteristics, such as their radius and critical current, are proposed as standards for field unit conversions. A proposed approach based on atomic interferometry could facilitate measurements with an estimated precision of $10^{-5}$ Gauss, which may have implications for fundamental research and the development of sensitive magnetic field detectors.

We have discovered a unique phenomenon with substrate-induced spin polarization in single-layer tungsten disulfide, where its thermal expansion behavior varies depending on the temperature. This occurrence is attributed to the symmetry difference between the WSe2 substrate and the tungsten disulfide layer, which gives rise to a spacially alternating spin polarization in tungsten disulfide. Moreover, this phenomenon is limited to layers bound to the substrate and we found that free-standing layers of tungsten disulfide display typical thermal expansion characteristics. This novel feature of tungsten disulfide could be utilized for detecting internal temperature distributions and we propose the use of Raman spectroscopy for monitoring this effect.

We investigate the effect of the electron spill-out and local-field corrections on the plasmons in nanogaps, focusing on the behavior as the gap width approaches zero. Using a rigorous quantum-mechanical approach, we find that the electron spill-out significantly amplifies the gap-plasmon frequency in small gaps, while the local-field corrections have a less pronounced impact. However, in ultra-small gaps (below 0.1 nanometers), the divergence of the electron density within the gap leads to a much more pronounced influence, dominating the behavior. Consequently, the choice of gap-model has a more substantial impact below this threshold, emphasizing the need for precise modeling in this range.

Type theory's intuitive progression, where types are normalized into a canonical form, is hindered by the complexity of the dependent lambda calculus, specifically due to the interplay between dependent types and product types. Normalization becomes circuitously achievable only by adhering to a specific order of reductions, which unfortunately leads to errors in evaluation attempts. Introducing a robust normalization system for the Dependent Lambda Calculus with Bar Induction, Agda-like Implication, and Empty Type, our approach involves modifying the strategy to allow for the normalization of a broader class of terms, which does not necessitate a predetermined reduction order. This results in a more coherent union of type theory components, avoiding the need for intricate normalization before attempted reduction.

This lecture will introduce students to fundamental concepts in topological quantum phenomena using the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. We will begin by presenting the SSH model and then explore its key characteristics in different scenarios, utilizing both numerical methods and analytical approaches. Through the SSH model, we will delve into the underlying principles of topological quantum physics, covering the aspects related to system symmetry, hinge modes, and fermionic properties, ultimately revealing the model's capacity to serve as a platform for the study and creation of topological phases.

Finite mixture models are examined in the context of statistical inference. It is shown that approximating models, which involve random variations, are more accurate than their deterministic counterparts. This improvement is achieved by using a measure that integrates over multiple point processes. The benefits of these stochastic mixture models are illustrated through examples in spatial statistics.

We derived the AdS$_5$ correction to a scalar's wave function in SUSY Yang-Mills theory, using the methods of finite temperature QFT. This involves calculating the temperature-dependent effective action for a scalar field with both the Weyl multiplet and the graviphoton included. The resulting AdS$_5$ correction to the wave function's temperature dependence was found to be in agreement with the type IIB string theory calculation, for the fundamental chiral primary operator of the $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory. Furthermore, we extended this calculation to the self-energy of a graviphoton field in the $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM theory, and found that it matches the type IIB string theory prediction. This involves showing that the self-energy is consistent with the AdS$_5$ correction to the dimension of the corresponding chiral primary operator, for both the fundamental and some higher rank operators.

High-performance computing on GPUs is predominantly object-based, yet the limited number of memory banks available leads to significant memory access conflicts.  As a result, the default memory manager in CUDA falls short in allocating memory efficiently for object-based codes.  To bridge this gap, we present DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocator designed to minimize memory access conflicts and high latency for memory re-allocation.  This memory manager uses a space-obtained-and-reclaimed strategy that dynamically divides memory into smaller blocks to reduce conflicts and latency.  DynaSOAr outperforms the default CUDA memory manager by a factor of two to five in various benchmarks.  Furthermore, it offers a free performance boost of the default CUDA memory manager.  DynaSOAr is an open-source project available on GitHub.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, calculations for a single manganese adatom and manganese clusters on the Nb(110) surface have been performed. By applying this framework to study the YSR states induced by a manganese adatom and manganese clusters within a relatively tight-binding surface sector, we gained valuable insights into their spectral properties. These findings are supported by experimental spectra obtained through high-resolution photoemission spectroscopy. By extending the theory to three-dimensional projections, excellent agreement is achieved for both a single manganese adatom and manganese clusters on Nb(110), further validating the applicability of the developed theory to more complex systems.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural surfaces to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict instance masks with boundary edges, especially in scenarios with multiple object instances and varying resolution levels. Since implicit surfaces are function-based, they can be easily graded to predict confidence levels for predicted masks, facilitating metric computation and multi-scale prediction. By integrating Fourier transformations with implicit surfaces, FourierMask outperforms Mask R-CNN at the same FPN level and matches state-of-the-art performance with simpler backbone models, while also exhibiting robust performance on the Cityscapes dataset. Code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/oguzeiytan/FourierMask.

Given a given natural number k and a differential manifold M, we can map M to a k-dimensional flat Euclidean space in a way that for every point in M, the curvature is bounded by some constant. If this mapping is not possible for any set of boundaries B, no matter how small, there exists a point in the manifold where the curvature at that point is greater than those boundaries. B determines a convex cone in the space of symmetric tensors on M. If the dimension of M is 2, we can use this convex cone to get an exact bound on the curvature at some point in the manifold. If the dimension of M is greater than 2, we can get a non-trivial bound on the curvature at some point in the manifold. If the dimension of M is greater than 2, we can get a non-trivial bound on the curvature at some point in the manifold, if the convex cone corresponding to B contains a finite number of flat immersions of submanifolds of M.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex, convectively formed clouds due to their opacity. This study introduces an innovative approach to breaking this limitation, using tomographic reconstruction from space-based observations. The method utilizes observations from the MISR and MODIS satellites, taking advantage of the wide viewing angles of MISR to gain vital information about the three-dimensional structure of clouds, even in their most intricate forms. By employing a nonlinear inverse problem solver, the technique reconstructs a three-dimensional volume from two-dimensional images, enabling the derivation of optical properties and determination of core regions hidden from view. The development of this method enables the discovery of previously invisible cloud cores, providing new insights into the physical processes occurring within these critical areas of clouds. The approach offers promising avenues for extending cloud retrieval to previously inaccessible types of clouds, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the interactions between clouds and energy in the Earth's system.

In this research, we utilized a spectral shift in laser energy (chirp) to speed up the ion acceleration produced by relativistic self induced transparency, increasing the charge state of ions by roughly 10 times over traditional methods. Our theoretical model and particle-in-cell simulations both reveal that a highly charged and energetically optimized ion beam can result from chirped laser interaction with neutral or weakly ionized materials, specifically demonstrating the potential of this technique to produce big gains in proton beam protons'energy and charge while maintaining a small thickness. A thoroughly investigated model is used to explain the underlying mechanism, attributing the increase in ion charge to a specific spectral shift that aligns with the critical frequency of electrons during the self induced transparency process.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions.

We examined the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately capture the complexities of this system, we applied a 56-atom supercell via first-principles calculations, leveraging a hybrid density functional theory framework.  The results indicate that substitutional carbon defects possess a marginal expansion in size, with no inherent magnetic properties, while a nitrogen atom bonded to three oxygen atoms forms a p-bond that cannot be stabilized by the band structure, instead requiring an extra nitrogen defect atom to form an N2 unit with isotropic properties.  Conversely, a nitrogen atom bonded to two oxygen atoms and one titanium atom forms a p$\sigma$ bond, with magnetic properties that arise from electron localization in an N-O-Ti chain, specifically in a 5$\sigma$ state, and can be stabilized in an N2 unit with anti-ferromagnetic interaction.  We found that both carbon and nitrogen defects can act as efficient electron-accepting dopants, with notable effects on photocatalytic activity under visible light.  The proposed N2 units offer a plausible explanation for persistent ferromagnetism in doped TiO2 systems.

One of the most well-established methods for detecting the higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider involves identifying the higgs production process where the higgs boson decays into two top quarks. However, this production process also allows for the possibility of the top quarks being produced in other forms, such as longitudinally coupled top quark pairs, or via tree-level processes such as top pair production via exchange of scalar di-quark operators, which could have a significant rate if the mass scale of the operator is high enough. Moreover, the LHC has a high enough energy to produce non-confined color fields between the two top quarks, potentially leading to the production of a longitudinal top quark pair bound by gluons, or via the realisation of a 1 GeV mass scale in the large-$(N_c-2)$ color combination, which could result in the production of two isolated top quarks. It has been observed that the existing searches at the LHC have insufficient sensitivity to detect such scenarios due to their high-degree of purity, and thus it is proposed that the existing top quark pair removal data by itself possesses a high enough sensitivity to detect the production of the longitudinal top quark pair, or the tree-level process of top pair production via exchange of scalar di-quark operators with a mass scale of the order of 100 GeV to several TeV, or the production of two isolated top quarks for the mass scale of the order of

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays offer a rich understanding of galaxy clusters' dynamics.  Maintaining equilibrium within the ICM is partially achieved by non-thermal pressure and the dissipation of turbulent energy.  However, the nature of ICM turbulence - its vectorial direction and scalar magnitude - remains unclear and needs further X-ray measurements.  Future missions like XARM or the next generation of X-ray telescopes will involve a fundamental transformation in the analysis of ICM turbulence using spatial structure functions of the ICM temperature.  The estimation of these structure functions from X-ray data, however, is subject to measurement uncertainties that are not yet considered in the estimation of turbulence maps.  The uncertainties of electron number density measurements affect the derivation of temperature increments, influencing the estimation of structure functions.  The current study measures these uncertainties for the first time and provides guidelines for the detectability of turbulent patterns.  The results show that the existing limitations of future missions like XARM will allow the detectable scaling of turbulent patterns at $\sim 10^8 M_\sun$ in mass.  The research offers a practical approach that can be used to assess the effectiveness of future missions in mapping turbulence and will be useful in its implementation.

In 1999, Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il and R\"odl introduced the concept of Ramsey upper richness to better understand Ramsey properties in infinite graphs. Over the past two decades, Ramsey upper richness has been extensively researched for various infinite graph families, including trees, infinite sequences of specific length, and certain types of infinite bipartite graphs. However, the Ramsey upper richness of general infinite graphs remained a significant unknown until recently. In this study, we investigated the Ramsey upper richness of graph factors obtained from multiple infinite graphs under different relation types, and we derived upper and lower bounds for their Ramsey numbers, depending on the specific factors.

Located in the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation of molecular gas. Recent studies have proposed that the CMZ is forming a ring-shaped pattern due to the influence of dynamical processes on rotating molecular gas. An analytical method has been developed to model the density of molecular gas within the CMZ by incorporating anisotropic factors, derived from 2D correlation functions of gas and star formations across the region. By applying this method and analyzing the data, researchers found that their model accurately predicts the anisotropic distribution of gas within the CMZ by identifying specific patterns. Furthermore, the model reveals a noticeable shift in the stellar component along the major axis of the CMZ, which is not evident in other directions. This discovery suggests that the anisotropic density framework is a crucial factor in understanding the formation of ring-like structures in the CMZ.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to detect Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing eye movements in a video. Unlike conventional methods relying on facial image analysis or patient-reported symptoms, this approach is non-invasive and effective even in the early stages of the condition. Through the collection of first-person video data, our system accurately identifies Bell's Palsy with a high degree of sensitivity and a low error rate, outperforming a pre-existing benchmark method. Notably, this detection method is also capable of identifying other facial nerve disorders.

Our study proposes using qudits of higher order, such as qutrits, to implement the holographic quantum fluid model, based on the quantum analog of spacetime with non-Minkowskian metrics. This involves rearranging the metric tensor to conform to the properties of the qudits, which enables a more efficient simulation of the model. We focus specifically on the noise characteristics of this system under local dephasing and erasure channels, which exhibit a unique, system-size-dependent behavior when simulated with qutrits. Unlike the two-dimensional case, where increasing noise with qudits also increases the system's size is not a critical factor. However, there is a critical qudit degree that maximizes the effect of noise on the system for higher dimensions.

In the field of laser physics, creating an abundance of polarized positrons through polarized electron targets under the influence of multi-TeraWatt mid-infrared lasers is a key area of study. To achieve this in a thin target, where the critical density is exceeded due to the combined effects of electron polarization and radiation pressure, a specific positron polarization state is produced as a result of quantum electrodynamic interactions. However, the traditional method of increasing the positron yield through thicker targets is limited by the increased imperfection fields that result from the increased Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities in the target, which also reduce the positron polarization. To overcome this limitation, we propose the use of a specific target design where a thin, iridium film is deposited on a glass substrate and then exposed to the laser, where the differences in the thermal expansion between the two materials cause a stress that generates a high magnetic field within the target. This results in an increased electric field due to the curvature of the electron trajectory, which in turn increases the positron yield by approximately five times with an accompanying increase in positron polarization. Notably, this design allows for the potential application of this technique to the study of laser-plasma interaction in the quantum electrodynamic regime with table-top lasers.

In this paper, we investigate the concept of a group having a polynomial-sized approximation to its largest invariant subgroup, focusing on finite groups. Specifically, we establish a criterion for a finite group to have a subnormal series of polynomial depth, relating this property to its largest normal subgroups. Additionally, we provide a characterizations for a finite group to have a subnormal series of polynomial width, and demonstrate that this condition is equivalent to there existing a normal subgroup in the group's permutation module, which can be computed efficiently. Building on this finding, we explore the implications for group actions on sets, showing that a polynomial-action is equivalent to having a normal subgroup in the permutation module, which further implies the existence of a semi-stable group action on sets of polynomial size.

This research develops a semi-analog temperature detection circuit using a single CMOS process, providing a wide operating range from 0.6V to 1.8V. The design utilizes a minimal number of active components, incorporating just one operational amplifier and two transconductance controllers. To facilitate digital temperature display, the circuit employs a hysteresis-based switching mechanism to generate multiple analog voltage levels in relation to temperature, with each conversion covering a 10°C range. As a result, the proposed temperature detector offers a digital temperature output capable of converting to Celsius scale with an error of less than 2°C. Built-around 0.18μm CMOS process, the integrated circuit occupies an area of 0.021mm² and features a power consumption of 10.6nW at 25°C.

In the case of stars with significant magnetic fields, where the presence of this field has a substantial impact on the circulation of matter, the Crocco-Stewart type relation holds. This relation essentially establishes a direct link between the velocity and temperature variations within the star, largely bypassing the need to account for magnetic forces when modeling this process. However, this method is only applicable if the magnetic field's influence is minimal, specifically in terms of flux expansion, which determines how the field's strength changes as it moves with the star's circulation patterns. If the magnetic field is highly confined, like in the case of a star with a surface temperature of around 300 Kelvin, its effect might be considerable, leading to possible instability. 

Using computational models, we simulated the internal and external magnetic forces at work in two variables related to the star's circulation: the equivalent specific angular momentum and the equivalent magnetic pressure. Our analysis shows that in the case of a 10.2 Solar mass star with a surface temperature of around 300 Kelvin, the magnetic pressure exhibits instability due to its high ratio of internal to external pressure. 

On the other hand, in a 0.5 Solar mass star with a surface temperature of around 250 Kelvin, both the magnetic pressure and equivalent specific angular momentum remain stable, largely adhering to the requirements set by the Crocco-Stewart relation.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) introduces a derivative expansion of the effective action, requiring the solution of fluid dynamics equations derived from Ward identities. By integrating the spatial derivatives, the focus shifts from the full derivative expansion, albeit preserving the underlying physical insights. In this study for zero-dimensional quantum field theories, we integrate the temporal derivatives, analogous to fluid dynamics in the limit of infinite viscosity, and develop a numerical approach to determine the leading irreducible corrections for interactions, utilizing the $O(N)$ model as a test case. Our study provides a precise, computationally efficient framework for evaluating the derivative expansion on a numerical level. By extending our methods to the imaginary time dimension, we obtain the leading irreducible corrections in the $d$-dimensional case. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the distinction between the $O(N)$ model's behavior in $d=2$ and $d=4$, reflecting well-known phenomena such as the Higgs phase and spontaneous symmetry breaking.

Music system evaluation typically relies on manual data assessment, 
which is resource-intensive and unfeasibly large for comprehensive coverage. 
In contrast, playing a game appears to be an effective and enjoyable method 
for thoroughly testing the capabilities of a music system, as it engages 
multiple system features simultaneously and across diverse contexts. 
Building upon this idea, we present Pied Piper, a modular music game 
designed for evaluation and training of music models, while also being 
playable and entertaining from a user perspective. 
By incorporating musical composition and variation goals within a 3D 
virtual world framework, Pied Piper presents multiple challenges and 
adventures that music systems can be assessed against, offering a more 
engaging and comprehensive evaluation framework than traditional methods. 
To facilitate seamless interaction with the game from different 
implementations of music systems, we introduce a straightforward text- 
based XML configuration for connecting systems to the game. 
To validate the effectiveness of Pied Piper, we conducted a series of user 
studies to compare the results of music system evaluation using the game 
versus traditional methods, showing that system rankings consistently 
correlate with player feedback obtained while playing the game. 
Furthermore, to make the game accessible to a wider range of music 
systems, we introduced an open API that enables the connection of systems 
from both research and commercial sources, while also developing multiple 
leaderboard competitions that reward high-performing music systems in various 
challenges.

We introduce a novel concept, geometric frameworks, which generalizes both the notion of Lie groupoids and geometric structures in a unified framework. This universal framework allows us to establish a categorical relationship between the set of geometric frameworks and the set of Lie groupoids, as well as between the set of geometric frameworks and the set of geometric structures. Furthermore, this relationship gives rise to a natural, universal concept of reduction for geometric frameworks, which encompasses both the reduction of Lie groupoids and the reduction of geometric structures.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with masses also exceeding the threshold for their own mass accumulation, indicating a process of mass growth.  Additionally, the velocity dispersion of protostellar cores is observed to be greater than in starless cores, a distinction that cannot be solely attributed to the influence of gravity.  This difference in velocity dispersion is suggestively linked to the potential for massive star formation in cores with outflows, with further support coming from the discovery of a significant correlation between the mass of these cores and the mass of young objects within them.  This relationship is found to break down in cores with outflows, with such cores instead following a different track that may indicate a distinct pathway to massive star formation.

Godel modal logics have proven useful in modeling intuitionistic and constructive reasoning for over 50 years. However, the lack of a clear algebraic foundation has hindered further development. To address this, our research develops a range of relational structures and algebras that accurately capture the semantics of Godel modal logics, building on the previous work of Janssen. These structures provide a foundation for applying tunnelling, a method for deriving results in the context of modal logic, and demonstrate that some Godel extensions possess finite, distributive lattices. This finding challenges the common assumption in the broader algebraic and logical community that distributive lattices are insufficient for modelling modal logic.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, enabling systematic observations of various ecological parameters. LiDAR data contains intricate information about forest canopies, allowing for the derivation of key biophysical variables such as species information, operational efficiency of photosynthesis, and plant water status. Despite the potential of LiDAR to complement traditional, labor-intensive field methods, a lack of advanced analysis techniques has limited its widespread adoption. In response, we present a platform that integrates machine learning into a standard LiDAR processing pipeline, increasing flexibility and performance. Through numerical testing, our integrated system demonstrates enhanced classification capabilities and processing speeds for multiple targets across various distances. The platform's effectiveness is further validated in real-world applications, showcasing improvements in performance and efficiency. By providing targeted services and promoting collaboration between remote sensing experts and data owners, we aim to facilitate the seamless integration of LiDAR data into the platform, ultimately benefiting the community through shared knowledge and advancements.

We're developing a new method for predicting future values in random processes on the sphere $S^{d}$, taking a step back from fully specified stochastic recurrence equations. This approach allows us to apply the method even when the underlying stochastic recurrence equations are not well defined. We've established conditions for the method to be feasible in cases when the processes are mean square bounded and have derived an optimal one-step predictor that minimizes the expected squared error. We've also found that the optimal one-step predictor corresponds to a specific recurrence equation that includes a stationary process on $S^{d}$ and a process that is independent and identically distributed. We've explored specific applications using processes that are independently and identically distributed and demonstrated that our method outperforms naive predictors. Furthermore, we've discovered that the optimal one-step predictor can be used to estimate stationary processes and proved the convergence of the method under certain conditions.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper presents results from a comprehensive search for spatial correlations between 460 neutrinos detected by IceCube and 40 UHECRs with energies above 60 EeV, resulting in no significant correlations within any distance or energy range. Additionally, when combining radio-detected UHECRs with energies above 50 EeV, two potential correlations with neutrino clusters were found, both exhibiting the expected UHECR-neutrino energy correlation seen in cosmological UHECR analyses.

The interaction between fluids and solid surfaces depends on factors like surface tension, viscosity, and how the surface is topped. Consider a surface with a texture, like a sponge or a surface with small holes in it, and compare it to a smooth surface. Research has shown that a smooth surface allows low-viscosity fluids to flow easily, while the same fluids flow much more quickly on a surface with small holes, due to the influence of the Plateau border. However, the way a surface with small holes affects fluids that have a high viscosity of about one centipoise is not as well understood. This phenomenon was studied with liquid foams of different viscosities, ranging from 1 centipoise to 100 centipoise, in a test that compared the flow on a smooth surface and a surface with small holes, specifically textured parallel bars. The results showed that high-viscosity fluids flow more quickly on a smooth surface than on a surface with small holes, which was found to be due to the high energy required to break the stiff walls of a foam layer as it flows over the textured surface. This effect was seen to be more pronounced with more viscous fluids and those that have a higher density of bubbles. It could have implications for the way we think about friction in fluids and how it is affected by the presence of surfaces with textures.

This report details the winners' approach in the first place during the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using imaging and metadata for skin cancer identification. A novel technique was presented, combining a convolutional neural network with an entropy-based method to correctly classify 1,012 samples out of 2,018 (50.5% accuracy). Notably, this approach excelled in detecting and discarding questionable samples, yielding superior results compared to the competition and baseline models.

The steady, fingerling pattern that develops in a horizontally extended Hele-Shaw cell, filled with a less dense and less viscous fluid, overdamped by a rotating viscous outer layer, experiences significant adjustment with increasing rotation.  Regardless of how high the rotation rate is, the fingerlings can easily change direction due to their flexibility, as evidenced by the finite Lyapunov exponent shown in the corresponding figure.  This behavior stands in contrast to the stiff, fingerlike patterns that emerge in similar experiments without rotation, as demonstrated by the diagram also presented in the figure.  The occurrence of this flexible state attribute can be explained by the revelation that the model possesses a family of stable, neutrally buoyant modes located within the inner cell, which provides a secure habitat for the fingerlings during the early stages of development.  This inner stability is later compromised by the arrival of the less dense, less viscous finger at the critical condition that defines the transition from the neutral to the charged state, leading to the capture of the neutrally buoyant mode and the resulting flexible fingerling.  This captures the functional reason for the rotation-induced shift from the rigid to the flexible state, as does the diagram of the phase diagram presented in the figure.

Building on a novel method which leverages Hamiltonian trajectories for microstate nonequilibrium calculations, we've adapted this approach for use in expanding systems. Due to the significant change in phase space volume during free expansion, conventional methods based on detailed balance can't be applied; the new method helps overcome this challenge. By transforming to a new Hamiltonian in the expanded phase space, we've successfully replicated nonequilibrium thermal expansion behavior using a technique that could also be relevant for understanding nonequilibrium dynamics in systems undergoing expansions similar to free expansion.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C$_{5}$H$_{5}$C$\equiv$N) a cyclopentadiene derivative, emanating from the TMC-1 direction, utilizing the ATLASfactory backend at the Subaru telescope's Submillimeter Wave Telescope (SMT). Ethynyl cyclopentadiene was initially discovered by multi-transitional molecular line observations, and further analysis of 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene led to the detection of 1-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene at a relative abundance of 0.25 in comparison to its isomeric counterpart, which could not be detected directly. Both molecules belong to the larger class of hydrocarbon cycles (HCCs), which comprise CCH and CN molecules, with ethynyl cyclopentadiene representing the smallest derivative of HCCs discovered so far. While previous studies have revealed the presence of larger derivatives such as indene and benzene in TMC-1, ethynyl cyclopentadiene offers a crucial test of the formation pathways of HCCs.
